the development of microarray-based methods to study aminocyclitol-containing antibiotics, which have been used for over half a century to treat bacterial infections, and their resistance to bacterial pathogens.

developing and using microarray-based methods to investigate the modification of aminocyclitols by enzymes that confer antibiotic resistance, and to study how such modifications affect their interactions with their targets, and with other proteins.
the development of new methods to study antibiotic resistance and the discovery of new antibiotics.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
these microarrays can provide a wealth of information about the structure and function of aminogylcoside antibiotics.

the arrays have been used to study the following aminoglycoide antibiotics and their modifications by resistance-causing aminoglycodases: kanamycin, paromomycin, gentamicin, neomycin, spectinomycin, streptomycin, tobramycin and hygromycin B.

the microarray-based methods developed here are useful for studying resistance to aminoglyoside antibiotics and for discovering new antibiotics that are not modified by aminoglycoide resistance-causing enzymes.

the use of aminogluconic acid (AGA) as a universal linker to immobilize aminogly-cosides on microarray surfaces enables a variety of studies to be carried out with the same microarray.
